newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU edges towards beef label agreement.
newsitem.headline: EU edges towards beef label agreement.

text.p: European Union farm ministers, anxious to restore consumer confidence shaken by the mad cow disease health scare, were edging towards agreement on Wednesday to label the origin of beef sold in shops from January 2000.

EU diplomats said Britain and Italy, the main opponents, were likely to accept a compromise drawn up by the Dutch EU Presidency offering an opt-out clause allowing a member state to apply the system on a voluntary basis on its territory.
"We have taken into account the special wishes of all countries concerned," a Dutch official said on the third day of the ministerial session.
The compromise provides greater flexibility, notably over time limits for farmers to report information on where cattle were born, raised and slaughtered for recording on computer data bases.
It provides a framework for beef labelling until the end of 1999, allowing those member states who wish to do so to introduce compulsory systems before 2000 for beef sold in their country.
Farm ministers would decide by the end of 1999 whether extra information should be put on beef labels and whether other meat products should be labelled.
British officials said agreement was now possible, provided a satisfactory outcome was reached on farmers' compensation for income losses caused by a strengthening currency.

Unanimity is required because the European Commission opposes Dutch plans to give the European Parliament only an advisory role instead of joint decision-making power over the creation of EU cattle identification and beef labelling systems.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler criticised the Dutch compromise because it reduced parliament's participation, greatly weakened the schemes and could create problems over imports from non-EU countries, a spokesman said.
"Consumers want more information. They want to know how the meat is produced," agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
Kiely added that Fischler refused to link beef labelling with compensation for exchange rate losses.
Britain, Italy and Ireland have recently undergone a series of revaluations which under existing rules would result in EU compensation of 1.8 billion ecus in 1998 and subsequent years.

The three countries say the proposal to limit aid is discriminatory because it did not apply to Germany and seven other countries which had revalued since the rules were introduced in 1993. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
